articles.title: 'Your legacy will live forever': Nepal mourns climber Nirmal Purja
articles.summary: Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed some of the country's best mountaineers.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Students and staff at Purja's former school lit candles in commemoration of him By Koh Ewe 
- Published 3 August 2026 
Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed all 10 members of an expedition on Pakistan's Broad Peak, six of whom were Nepalese. 
Among them was Nirmal Purja, also known as Nims, a British-Nepali climber most known for climbing the world's 14 tallest peaks in just over six months. 
His death has sent shockwaves through the global mountaineering community and through Nepal, where he is a celebrated figure for giving a spotlight to Nepali climbing guides. 
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah was among those who paid tribute, saying his "history of courage, dedication and contribution will always remain inspiring". 
In a moving tribute on Facebook, Purja's brother Kamal wrote: "I feel as though I have lost my whole world. My brother was not only my younger brother - he was my heart." 
"Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added. 
At the Small Heaven School in Chitwan district, near Kathmandu, which Purja had once attended, students and staff lit candles and mourned his death. 
Sarbagya Paudel, one of the students at the vigil, said Purja's "bravery has set a great example for our school. Not only has he made our school proud, but he has also brought pride to Nepal". 
Purja is still fondly remembered by those who had known him from his schooling days. Shailendra Baral, his school hostel supervisor, told AFP that as a young boy Purja had been "fearless and committed to achieving something". 
"He was honest and an obedient student, which made us happy. We found courage in him even when he was a child." 
Bahadur Panta, Purja's school friend, said he had prayed for the mountaineer through "sleepless nights" after news broke of his disappearance. 
"It was not only me and my friends. I think people all over the world who knew him... prayed for him. But it was his fate, no one could avoid it," he told AFP. 
Social media was also awash with tributes to Purja, with many saying that Nepal was in mourning and that the country had lost a "legend" and "many great climbers". 
"Their legacy will live on," said one comment. 
Purja was catapulted into international stardom after his journey was documented in a 2021 Netflix documentary. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Bahadur Panta was a friend of Purja's in school 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
He was among dozens that gathered at the Small Heaven school in Chitwan 
Among his 10-member expedition on Broad Peak, there were six Nepali climbers. The other four climbers were from the US, China, Oman, Pakistan. 
They had gone missing after being caught in an avalanche last Thursday on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak. 
Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit. 
Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives. 
Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering. 
Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military. 
But as he became more famous, troubling allegations emerged about his conduct. 
In 2024, a New York Times article detailed sexual allegations two women made against Purja. One alleged that he had sexually assaulted her in a hotel room in 2023 and another said he had grabbed and propositioned her while guiding her on an expedition to K2 in 2022. He denied these claims through his lawyer.

But while Purja may be the most recognisable face, he was not the only famed climber in the disaster-hit expedition on Broad Peak. The 10-member team also consisted of big names in Nepal's climbing community. 
There was Pur Bahadur Gurung - also known as Yukta - who summitted Everest 10 times. In 2024, he was part of the team that discovered a century-old shoe on the world's tallest peak, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on Everest with George Mallory in 1924. 
"Standing with you on the summit of Mount Everest is a memory I will cherish forever," fellow mountaineer and guide Uttam Lapraki wrote in a tribute to Yukta on social media. 
"The Himalayas have lost one of their finest sons, but your courage, kindness, and legacy will continue to inspire generations of climbers." 
Another member of the team, Kili Pemba Sherpa, was part of a historic 2021 expedition that summitted K2, the world's second-highest peak, in winter. That expedition was made up of all Nepali climbers, including Purja. 
Imagine Nepal, an expedition company where Kili Pemba worked as a guide, wrote on Instagram that he had "stood with us from the very beginning, from the days we first started climbing together". 
"He was humble in every way and never tired of helping climbers when they needed him. He was a foundation of our team and a part of every summit we have ever celebrated."

articles.title: Five dead and 41 missing after Indonesia ferry catches fire
articles.summary: The vessel with at least 250 people on board caught fire off Madura island.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Footage shows thick plumes of smoke billowing from Indonesia ferry By Olivia Ireland 
- Published 2 August 2026 
Five people have been found dead and 41 are missing after an Indonesian ferry carrying at least 250 people caught fire while at sea, officials say. 
The captain of the ship reported the fire - off Madura island - as the vessel sailed from the country's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, to Makassar in South Sulawesi, according to Basarnas, the National Search and Rescue Agency. 
Footage played by local Indonesian news outlet iNews shows large numbers of people in life jackets on what appears to be a lifeboat. 
Other clips show people climbing down from the ferry that has flames and plumes of smoke coming from the top of the vessel. 
Basarnas posted a video to its TikTok, with a statement saying at 08:24 (02:24 GMT) the Surabaya Search and Rescue office received information that passenger ship KMP Mutiara Sentosa 2 was on fire. 
"Based on information from the shipping company, the fire occurred at around 06:00-07:00 (00:00-01:00 GMT)." 
Later, Basarnas said it got confirmation the ferry "was almost entirely engulfed in flames" as "passengers held on in the ship's bridge and bow while awaiting rescue". 
It was unclear how the ferry caught fire, the statement said. 
In some of the footage, can be seen jumping into the sea, with crowds of people in life jackets gathering and lifebuoys being thrown to some before they are carried into a rescue ship.

articles.title: UK rapper Yung Filly found not guilty of raping woman after Australian show
articles.summary: The YouTuber has been found guilty for two counts of assault over the 2024 incident in Perth.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
UK rapper Yung Filly found not guilty of raping Australian woman By Katy Watson Australia correspondent 
- Published 31 July 2026 
UK rapper Yung Filly has been found not guilty of raping a fan after performing at a nightclub in Australia in 2024. 
On Friday a jury in Western Australia found him not guilty for three counts of sexual penetration without consent. 
But he was found guilty for two counts of assault occasioning bodily harm. 
The YouTuber, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, had been accused of sexually assaulting the woman, then 20 years old, in his hotel room after he performed in Hillarys, a coastal suburb of Perth. 
The jury could not come to a decision on three other counts of rape. 
Barrientos was also found not guilty for one count of assault occasioning bodily harm and also for strangulation. 
The 30-year-old social media star, who pleaded not guilty to all charges, cried when the verdict was read out, local media reported. 
He will remain on bail until 21 August, when the court will decide his sentencing date. 
Prosecutors will also decide on the next steps for the three hung jury verdicts - whether to press ahead or not on those rape charges. 
Barrientos has been on bail since being charged and was allowed to fly home to the UK in September for four months, before returning to Western Australia ahead of his trial. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The 30-year-old is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad 
Differing arguments 
During the trial, Barrientos had told the court that he had "fancied" the woman when they met at the concert venue. 
Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, had been in the VIP area while she leaned over the barrier from the general area. 
He denied touching her inappropriately. 
"I recall putting my hand on her waist," he told the court. But he said he had not put his hands down her pants or touched her breast. 
He said the "vibes were good" between him and the woman when they arrived at his hotel later. 
His security guard took the woman's phone away - "standard practice" to protect their privacy, according to Barrientos. 
The court heard that the pair had engaged in consensual sex in his hotel room before Barrientos turned violent and the young woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told him to stop. 
The woman accused the social media star of biting, bruising and even trying to choke her. Photos of bruises and bite marks on her face and neck were shown in court. 
Barrientos denied the woman had repeatedly asked him to stop, but did acknowledge that he bit her several times, explaining that he gave her a "love bite". 
During the trial's closing arguments, prosecutor Danielle Clarke said Barrientos was an "entitled" man with a "moderate degree of fame" who had violated the fan "in the most intrusive way possible". 
His defence lawyer argued that the accuser's evidence was full of "inconsistencies, embellishments and outright lies". 
Barrientos is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad, and has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows. 
In addition to his 1.8 million YouTube subscribers, he has three million followers on TikTok and and 2.4 million on Instagram.

articles.title: Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle: 'We are not lonely'
articles.summary: A growing number of so-called "loneliness influencers" are spotlighting solo living without children or friends - and it's spurring debate.
articles.full_text:
Image source, @lanasololife/@dramafreediaries/@devonandwillo Image caption, 
Content creators sharing the peace of solo living is making the rounds on social media By Yang Tian 
- Published 2 August 2026 
It's a Friday night. A young woman trudges back to her apartment after a day of work. She enters a spotless kitchen, unloads a bag of groceries, and unwraps a frozen pizza before sliding it in the oven. 
What follows is a nightly routine that is almost meditative in its mundanity: she lights a candle and gazes briefly at the snow-covered landscape outside her window, piles a premade salad onto a plate with the pizza, and settles on her sofa to eat in front of the TV. 
The tagline that accompanies the scene reads: "POV you're a childfree and single girl that has no friends and lives alone so this is how you spend your Friday night." 
At the centre of the video – which has amassed seven million views on TikTok – is Lana Isa, a software sales manager in her 20s based in Toronto. 
In addition to chronicling her nightly self-care routines, she takes her almost 400,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram on late-night fast food drives, reading sessions perched on a rock by the lake, even a saga of getting locked out of her apartment in the middle of the night. 
Isa is part of a growing, albeit niche corner of the internet where content creators, many of them women, share their daily rituals of living alone, choosing to spotlight a lifestyle that prioritises peace and solitude - the antithesis of social media excess. 
For Isa, unveiling the "no friends" aspect of her life was less of a tagline, but the "reality" she had been living for several years. 
Alone, but not lonely 
Image source, @lanasololife Image caption, 
Lana Isa says her videos show her real life and were never intended to "romanticise having no friends" 
After switching several high schools, enduring Covid isolation during her college years and moving across the country following her first heartbreak, Isa found herself forced to adjust to living alone with no close friends. 
"People don't talk about having no friends a lot... I think it's still what people would consider embarrassing or a little taboo," she says. 
When she started sharing the friendlessness of her circumstances on social media, an audience began to connect. Her initial following of around 2,000 followers on TikTok swelled to more than 175,000 in the span of eight months. 
"It was eye-opening to see other people who are living the same situation that I've been… and to feel like I could kind of relate to people for the first time in a while." 
And relate they did. Isa's comments section filled with people bonding over similar experiences of living alone or having no friends, and finding comfort in "feeling seen". 
Figure caption, 
Alone not lonely: Meet the women building community through solitude 
As with most trends online, curiosity quickly turned to backlash. Isa and similar creators were dubbed "loneliness influencers", with some framing them as part of a new demographic of sad, lonely, childless women in crisis. 
Others accused them of romanticising self isolation and encouraging an "air of cosy defeatism" by shunning social connections. 
But their reels paint a lifestyle that may be more relatable than many would care to admit. These women take themselves on solo dates, embark on spontaneous road trips, and even push through the awkwardness of attending parties alone. 
Destigmatising loneliness 
For Devon Noehring, a full-time content creator and self-proclaimed introvert based in Phoenix, Arizona, it's been "frustrating" to see her solo weekends cooking and lounging at home with her dog reduced to a symptom of female loneliness. 
"It's the exact opposite intention of our videos," she says. "I just hate the stigma of alone equalling lonely." 
While Noehring does have a close group of friends, growing up she always felt "ashamed" of being the quiet girl with social anxiety. It wasn't until she confessed her insecurities online that she discovered a following of fellow introverts who identified with her struggles. 
"Being alone is where I feel my most free and most like myself," she says. "That's how I recharge, and I feel very proud of myself for being independent and doing things alone… I think it's something that should be celebrated." 
Image source, @devonandwillo Image caption, 
Devon Noehring says her content is about prioritising her peace and asks, "What about this is sad to you?" 
Some health researchers have been working to "destigmatise loneliness" by differentiating between chronic loneliness forced by circumstance and those who have agency to choose to live and spend time alone. 
"Everybody's lonely at some point, but some people are not OK admitting that," says Professor Melody Ding, an epidemiologist researching social connection and loneliness at the University of Sydney. "That can create this false expectation that you have to be socially happy and connected all the time." 
But she cautions that while influencers can make being alone look "really appealing", humans still need social connection and it can be detrimental to one's mental and physical wellbeing to be stuck in a cycle of intense isolation. 
"We're a social species," says Ding. "We survive better with companionship, with people around us." 
She acknowledges that people's social needs vary at different stages of life, but Ding's hope for those who have lost relationships is that they can eventually "de-emphasise" the friendless aspect of their lives and forge new social bonds. 
"It's important we have people in our life and it's important these relationships are positive and nourish our lives," Ding adds. 
'We want to find people we relate to' 
Even in moments when they do feel lonely, these women say loneliness doesn't define their lives, nor do they aspire to remain permanently friendless. 
"We never describe ourselves as lonely," says SJ Hoadley, who works as a cleaner in the UK and began documenting her own solo living after discovering Isa's videos. "I think sometimes my lack of friends tends to bother the people around me more than it bothers me." 
After leaving a seven-year abusive relationship, she moved to a new area where she knew no one and was confronted with having to rebuild her life. Despite the initial "shock", she eventually started "enjoying and embracing that independence" and "getting to feel comfortable with my own company". 
Image source, @dramafreediaries Image caption, 
SJ Hoadley calls herself an "accidental influencer" and never expected to gain such a huge following 
In a social media ecosystem that thrives on flooding our feeds with aspirational living and a perennial state of FOMO (fear of missing out), the rise of solo living influencers can be validating for those who see themselves reflected in the lifestyle, says Dr Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch at the University of Connecticut who specialises in how humans build community online. 
"There's been this kind of long growing backlash against the idea that we're seeing everybody's perfect life, their highlight reel," she says. 
Oeldorf-Hirsch believes the appeal of solitude content is filling a social need for the creators and their audience, providing some "balance" against the dominance of hyper-glamourised influencer culture. 
"We're kind of trending towards these influencers that are more authentic, living their true life," she says. "We just want to find people we relate to." 
Hoadley has seen her following surge at times by tens of thousands per day, while Noehring's videos have garnered millions of views across her channels. 
Those online connections have made Hoadley excited for a future where she finds a "little group of girlfriends". Noehring hopes to one day organise a real world meet-up with her virtual community, and Isa says the support has given her the "push" she needed to start thinking about making friends again. 
"I think that what all the content is saying is: find your path," says Hoadley. "It doesn't have to be this one-size-fits-all that we keep getting pushed on social media."

A lithography machine at ASML in Veldhoven, the Netherlands. The Chinese have broken the Dutch company’s hold over deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain. Photograph: Bart van Overbeeke Fotografie/AS/Reuters 
View image in fullscreen 
A lithography machine at ASML in Veldhoven, the Netherlands. The Chinese have broken the Dutch company’s hold over deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain. Photograph: Bart van Overbeeke Fotografie/AS/Reuters Analysis 
Stock market turmoil sheds stark light on the opaque AI economy
Aisha Down , Dan Milmo and Graeme Wearden 
Investors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakers 
Even for the rollercoaster world of AI, last week was particularly volatile as investors scrambled to keep up with developments that threatened the dominance of the largest western chipmakers. 
It began with a double whammy. On Monday, the Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT floated on the Shanghai stock market, soaring by 466% in value to 3.3tn yuan (£365bn). 
That same day, it was reported that China had developed its own tools to carry out deep-ultraviolet lithography, a technique essential to the computer chip supply chain over which the Dutch company ASML had held a monopoly. 
AI-linked shares, particularly chipmakers, dropped around the world, sending many indices sliding. South Korea’s main share index, the Kospi, fell 11.5% on Tuesday and a further 6% on Wednesday , dragged down by its two biggest companies – the semiconductor maker SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. 
On Thursday, the main US tech index, the Nasdaq, fell into correction territory at one point after dropping more than 10% from its recent high, before easing back. Nvidia lost more than 5% by Thursday evening, by which time it had been overtaken by Apple as the world’s largest listed company . 
The next day there was a big rebound, when strong financial results from Amazon and Microsoft calmed traders’ nerves. The Kospi jumped nearly 20% – although the week’s slump still means it recorded its worst month since the height of the global financial crisis in October 2008. 
So, what exactly do these advances mean, and why have they got western investors so jittery? 
CXMT’s debut is impressive. But the company is arguably more of a boon to the global AI economy than a threat. It makes dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips, which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations. 
There is a global shortage of Dram chips, which is why phones and computers are expected to get far more expensive . Crucially, they are not graphics processing units (GPUs) – which are the key chips and the “brains” in an AI system. 
This means, put simply, that CXMT is not a threat to GPU maker Nvidia, the biggest company in the AI economy and the only one making a profit on AI. They produce complementary, not competing goods. 
View image in fullscreen 
China’s president, Xi Jinping, speaks at the opening of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Beijing. China is making rapid advances in the semiconductors used to drive AI. Photograph: Greg Baker/AFP/Getty Images 
The Chinese company could be a threat to SK Hynix and Micron, which do make memory chips. However, Alvin Nguyen, an analyst at the research firm Forrester, said the sell-off in these shares was an “overreaction” given that the global memory chip shortage is likely to continue until 2030. 
“SK Hynix, Micron, others, they can’t produce enough memory chips to begin with … the demand keeps growing even higher,” Nguyen said. 
A more serious concern could be the news that China can make the lithography tools. These are essentially extremely precise lasers that allow chipmakers to etch the thinnest lines in the world into wafers of silicon. 
Until now, only ASML could manufacture such machines. If this week’s reports are correct, Beijing could – in theory – produce GPUs that rival Nvidia’s. This would spell trouble for the world’s biggest company, and therefore Wall Street. But a serious competitor is still years away. 
“Fabs [semiconductor fabrication plants], as I know them, still take years to develop,” said Nguyen. 
Mark Boost, the chief executive of the UK cloud company Civo, agreed. “Investors are overreacting to the short-term threat,” he said. “Manufacturing a handful of [deep-ultraviolet] machines is a massive symbolic victory, but not a commercial replacement for ASML overnight. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
“Fabs run on efficiency and yield, and until these Chinese tools can match western reliability, ASML’s global dominance remains structurally safe outside mainland China.” 
Long term, this week’s advances are gamechanging for the AI economy, although in many ways they should have been predictable. Given US export controls, China has had little choice but to develop domestic capabilities . 
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, an online share trading company, said: “These Chinese chip companies appear poised to do to the big chipmakers what they have done to steel, automobiles and a host of other industries, namely undercut them and outcompete them on price.” 
It may be that last week’s correction is an overreaction – but also a reasonable response to a circular and extremely opaque AI economy that rests heavily on the fate of a single company, Nvidia. 
Its shares are gradually creeping up again, although they are still below what they were last week. A contributing factor to the investor skittishness appears to be yet another circular, opaque deal. 
Last Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was considering providing a $250bn (£186bn) backstop to OpenAI for a large datacentre project. This comes roughly half a year after a $100bn deal between the two companies fell apart . 
It was a significant factor in Nvidia’s decline over the week, according to Morningstar . The anxiety that underlies this is that the company has become the “ central bank of AI ” – holding up vast parts of the economy, and the global stock market, in ways that most people, investors included, do not understand. 
Many believe that it cannot last. What is on the other side is less clear. 
“Nvidia knows the gravy train’s going to run out,” Nguyen said. “Everybody’s waiting for them to fall apart. I don’t know that they will because what they do still has value … at some point in the future, they’ll no longer be one of the most valuable companies in the world. Maybe … they’ll be worth only $2tn. It’s still pretty good.”

China has banned hidden retractable car door handles. How are they dangerous – and what will Australia do?
The handles, which were popularised by Elon Musk’s Tesla EVs, have a record of failing and trapping passengers inside burning vehicles during deadly accidents

They used to be a novelty in Australia: the futuristic, flush-mounted car door handles favoured by Elon Musk’s Tesla. 
However while the design – popularised with the Tesla Model S in 2012 and since adopted by other manufacturers – might look sleek, it may not be great in an emergency. 
After several deadly high-profile accidents involving different makes and models, in which power failings saw people trapped inside the vehicle, China has announced a world-first ban on hidden or retractable electric car door handles. China to ban hidden car door handles on all EVs over crash safety concerns 
Read more 
But with less than six months to go before the ban is implemented, and domestic demand for electric vehicles booming, experts say it’s time for Australia to adopt the same precautions. 
What is changing?
While hidden door handles are used by car manufacturers around the world, they are particularly popular in China. As of April 2026, about 60% of the country’s 100 bestselling “new-energy vehicles” – EVs, hybrids or fuel cell-powered cars – had them, according to the China Daily. 
From 1 January 2027, all new cars sold in China will be required to have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of every door except the boot, according to regulations announced in February by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. 
Under the changes, on the outside of every door there must be a recessed space measuring at least 6cm by 2cm by 2.5cm for a hand to grasp the handle and manually open the door. On the inside, there must be signs showing occupants how to manually open the door. 
The ban will apply to both press-to-release hidden handles and electrical pop-out or retractable handles, Bloomsberg reported . 
The idea is that people will be able to open a car from the inside or outside in an emergency, even if the handle has lost power. 
Some manufacturers whose new models have already been approved for sale have been given a two-year grace period to update their designs. 
Tesla had already flagged design changes. In September last year, the company’s chief of design, Franz von Holzhausen, told Bloomberg it was looking to combine the electronic and manual door-release mechanisms , to make them more intuitive for occupants in “a panic situation”. 
What does this mean for Australia?
Australia imports all its cars, and there has been a recent influx of Chinese-made EVs due to their relative affordability. 
“About 60% of all new vehicles sold in Australia are made in China but that’s because they’re very good at making cars now, and Australians love a bargain,” says Chris Jones from the Australian Electric Vehicle Association (AEVA). 
Every car in the Top 10 EVs sold in May this year was primarily built in China, with manufacturers Tesla, Jaecoo, Geely, BYD and Zeekr behind the top models, according to Carsguide . 
Jones says the Chinese ban won’t extend to flush mounted door handles that can still be operated manually, which are the kind typically seen in Australia, so the ban may not apply to models currently popular in the country. 
However, Jones says it’s a good time to reconsider the Australian Design Rules – the national standards governing vehicle safety, anti-theft and emissions. 
“I think there is a perfectly reasonable case to mandate a manual mechanism on both inside and outside the vehicle for front and rear doors,” he says. 
“The Chinese government has recognised this flaw and the potential for disaster when extracting casualties from a crash, so are regulating accordingly.” 
What are the rules in Australia now?
A spokesperson for the transport minister, Catherine King, says all road vehicles, including EVs, must have doors that can be opened without the use of tools. In practice, this means all car door must be operational by hand. 
Although vehicles are tested for this function after both side and frontal impact crashes, this only applies to the outdoor handles as “there is usually no way to test the internal door handle following a crash test” using a dummy. 
King’s spokesperson says the government has provided the independent safety assessor Ancap with $16.3m in funding over 5 years to increase their door handle assessment as part of their Star Safety Rating Program. 
Carla Hoorweg, the Ancap chief executive officer, says the Australian Design Rules haven’t kept up with technology and don’t prescribe enough detail. 
“That’s what we want to make sure the rules are really clear on – that there has to be a manual override from the inside and the outside,” she says. “It’s both, so that occupants can get out and so first responders can get into the vehicle. 
“The objective is reducing the risk of entrapment after a crash.” 
Guardian Australia has contacted Tesla for comment. 
Will cars banned in China be “dumped” in Australia?
The issue made headlines again earlier this month after the peak body for car and truck dealers – the Australian Automotive Dealers’ Association – released a report warning of the “risk of stock dumping following China’s approach to EVs with flush door handles”. 
While cars rejected by the Chinese are unlikely to be literally “dumped” here – their steering wheels would be on the wrong side for Australian roads – Hoorweg says there is a risk that cars with less safe door handles could end up being sold here. 
“If there’s a lot of door handles floating around and they’re cheap because they can’t sell them in China, what are you going to do with them?” she says.

China’s tech advances are causing chaos from Silicon Valley to the White House
New AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industry 
O ver the past month, a series of advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled financial markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left the Trump administration scrambling to respond. 
Silicon Valley has long pointed to China’s tech industry as a competitive threat and used its growth as rationale for why US firms should not face regulatory oversight that could slow them down. In recent weeks, however, China’s progress has pushed US tech CEOs past vague warnings and into open disagreement over how to address Chinese-made products upending their industry. 
The most immediate threat to Silicon Valley’s status quo has come from a series of Chinese-made open-source, open-weight AI models that are free to download and use. The models, such as Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, are powerful enough to compete in some applications with proprietary and comparatively expensive AI products from OpenAI and Anthropic. 
The emergence of China’s open-source AI alternatives has caused divisions in both the White House and US tech industry over whether to oppose or embrace these new models. On one side are chip manufacturers who see revenue opportunities from increased AI usage and tech companies concerned about OpenAI and Anthropic’s growing dominance in the AI industry. On the other is Anthropic and OpenAI, which face profit pressures from open source models and argue that Chinese-made models pose security risks . 
The White House is similarly divided, historically hawkish on China’s tech industry but wary of blocking low-cost AI models that American businesses have come to rely on. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent suggested in recent weeks that the US could sanction Chinese AI firms over alleged intellectual property theft from American companies, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick has received letters from tech-startup founders asking him not to cut off access to open models. 
Amid reports that the Trump administration was considering banning or limiting the use of China’s open source models, a swath of prominent big tech companies including Microsoft, Nvidia, Palantir and Meta also recently published a letter urging lawmakers to refrain from putting restrictions on open models. Additionally, Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang went to Capitol Hill on Tuesday to meet with Democratic and Republican party leaders to lobby in support of open models. 
While facing heat from China and other tech companies, OpenAI and Anthropic revealed in recent weeks that their AI models went rogue during cybersecurity tests and hacked into outside organizations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited lawmakers and administration officials this week to discuss controls on AI following the incident. That forced Donald Trump to field questions about whether he would put more safety restrictions on AI development. 
“We have to be careful in both ways. We don’t want to restrict them when all of a sudden we come in second to China,” Trump said, adding: “I know many of these people. I don’t want to restrict them from doing great work.” 
While the Trump administration debates potential safety controls and limits on Chinese-made AI models, it took tangible action this week against China’s increasingly prominent robotics industry. The Federal Communications Commission announced on Tuesday a ban on humanoid robots from China over what it alleged was an unacceptable national security risk. 
China’s humanoid robots from companies such as Unitree have been the subject of numerous viral videos this year, showcasing their ability to dance or interact with people when programmed to do so. The FCC alleged that the robots could also steal data or surveil US citizens, as well as threaten US manufacturing and supply chains. skip past newsletter promotion

The FCC’s decision further escalates the US competition with China over emerging technologies and comes as fears over China’s tech have shifted financial markets. A report from the Information this week stating that China had begun mass production of specialty chips key to the AI boom spurred a stock selloff that erased $1tn in market value from other chip manufacturers. 
As Chinese-made tech advancements increasingly begin to rival their US counterparts, Silicon Valley’s divisions could intensify, markets could become more skittish and the Trump administration could face more pressure over how to counter China’s influence.

articles.title: World-renowned climber Nirmal Purja among 11 struck by avalanche on Pakistan mountain
articles.summary: Rescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descentThe world-renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja – a former British special forces member – is among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.The Alpine Club of Pakistan said “seven climbers have been spotted via aerial drone footage” adding that “their identities and condition cannot yet be verified”. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Nirmal Purja had been leading an expedition on Broad Peak along with climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, Oman, China and the US. Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PA 
View image in fullscreen 
Nirmal Purja had been leading an expedition on Broad Peak along with climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, Oman, China and the US. Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PA 
World-renowned climber Nirmal Purja among 11 struck by avalanche on Pakistan mountain
Rescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descent 
The world-renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja – a former British special forces member – is among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. 
The Alpine Club of Pakistan said “seven climbers have been spotted via aerial drone footage” adding that “their identities and condition cannot yet be verified”. 
Rescuers had said earlier on Friday that four bodies had been found and efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Three of the dead have been identified: Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepali citizen, Nadhira Alharthy, who was the first Omani to climb Everest, and US climber Mallory Geis. Their bodies have been transported to a hospital. 
Purja, also known as Nims Dai, made history in 2019 after climbing all of the world’s 14 peaks over 8,000 metres in just over six months, cutting years off the previous record. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain in winter, a highly coveted achievement. 
View image in fullscreen 
Nirmal ‘Nims’ Purja and his Project Possible team are congratulated after successfully scaling all 14 mountains above 8,000 metres in just over six months. Photograph: Skanda Gautam/Zuma Wire/Rex/Shutterstock 
Purja has also attracted controversy, however, including a high-profile claim, which he denied , of sexually inappropriate behaviour. 
Also among those missing are the US climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese national, Wang Zhong, and Pakistani and Nepali high-altitude workers. 
As night fell on the mountain on Friday, visual searches for any survivors, including with the use of drones, were halted. Search efforts have been hampered by the weather and the fact that unlike in Nepal, where there is a well-established network of private helicopter search and rescue operations, helicopters are less available in Pakistan and run by the military. Map showing location of Broad Peak 
Trackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. 
The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camp two and camp three on the mountain’s west ridge, the most popular ascent route. 
According to Climbing magazine , Geis’s tracker showed a sudden descent of 543 metres, while Alharthy’s tracker showed a much-larger descent of 1,651 metres. 
View image in fullscreen 
Broad Peak, on the border of Pakistan and China, is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8,047 metres. Photograph: Naveed Hussain/Alamy 
Commenting on the rescue efforts, a spokesperson for police in the mountainous Gilgit-Baltistan region said “preliminary reports indicate that four bodies have so far been recovered”, adding that the condition of the remaining climbers was still being verified. 
A statement by the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) suggested an avalanche had struck a group of climbers around midday on Thursday. “The entire team has been out of communication since the avalanche,” the statement said, as teams with helicopters and drones were sent to help with rescue efforts. 
The statement added: “Every possible effort is being made to ensure that helicopter support and all available rescue resources are mobilised at the earliest opportunity, subject to weather and operational conditions.” 
Irfan Arshad Khan, the ACP’s president, said: “We can confirm the death of three climbers, as we received two dead bodies and a body part of another climber.” 
Purja’s business partner, Mingma Gyabu Sherpa, who is also a member of the Nepali house of representatives, said data appeared to show continuing movement from Purja’s tracking device after the initial incident. 
“Initially, it appeared that he had been swept downhill by the avalanche,” he told the Nepali news site Kantipur. “But after the point where the tracking had stopped, the location appears to have shifted again.” 
Mingma added that one Pakistani and one Nepali climber had set out overland towards the suspected avalanche site to check reports that one climber’s location appeared to be near the base of the mountain. 
“We have received information that one person’s location appears to be near the foot of the mountain. A search team has gone there to verify it,” he said. 
Mingma cautioned that they did not have any indication of Purja’s condition, simply that the location of the tracker had shifted. 
In person, Purja was striking for his confidence and self-belief . His rapid chain of ascents of the world’s tallest mountains demonstrated strength and a talent for logistical organisation, using the exploit to showcase what he felt were the overlooked abilities of Nepali climbers. 
His profile was boosted after he starred in a 2021 Netflix documentary on the feat. The previous record for climbing all 14 was seven years; his record was surpassed in 2023. 
View image in fullscreen 
Purja, after being part of the all-Nepali mountaineering team that became the first to scale K2 in winter, arrives at Tribhuwan international airport in Kathmandu in January 2021. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP 
Purja was leading an expedition for his company, Elite Exped, on Broad Peak, the world’s 12th-highest mountain at 8,047 metres, when the avalanche occurred. 
The ACP received “deeply concerning” reports on Thursday that an avalanche had struck the team. ‘It’s not about ego’, says speed climber who tamed world’s 14 highest peaks 
Read more 
The expedition includes five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said the ACP’s vice-president, Karrar Haidri. 
“The club prays for the safety and successful rescue of all the climbers and stands in solidarity with their families and the international mountaineering community during this difficult time,” the ACP said in a statement. 
View image in fullscreen 
Nims Purja on Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest mountain, in Nepal Photograph: Supplied 
Purja, who is also a British citizen after joining the British army in 2003, opted to use supplementary oxygen for his ascents, justifying his choice by the huge size of the challenge he had set himself. 
Purja had written on X this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 mountains over 8,000 metres twice without oxygen. “Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down,” he wrote. “I take zero mountains for granted. Not one. The moment my foot leaves basecamp, it’s 100%. Always has been. Always will be. 
“My purpose has never been about me. It’s about what I represent. It’s about showing YOU that your own mountains – whatever they are – are climbable.”

Chinese super-embassy in London to go ahead after high court challenge dismissed
Royal Mint Court residents’ association, which sought to stop planning permission, says it will appeal against ruling 
Construction of a controversial new Chinese embassy was given the green light on Friday after the high court dismissed a challenge from neighbours. 
The Royal Mint Court residents’ association (RMCRA), which brought the case against the government, immediately announced plans to appeal against the decision, in a move that could cause further delays to the project. The debate over planning permission for the new embassy has been a sore point of British-Chinese relations in recent years. 
The RMCRA represents people and businesses who live and operate from properties in Royal Mint Court, the historic site that the Chinese government bought for £255m in 2018. 
The association argued that the government had been unlawful in granting planning permission and that it had failed to assess the human rights considerations of the project. 
In January the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government gave permission for China to build the vast new diplomatic outpost, which would be Beijing’s biggest in Europe. 
The decision was delayed for months after the planning application was taken out of the hands of the local council, Tower Hamlets, which had originally rejected it on security grounds. Senior spy officials later advised the government that the risks to UK national security could be controlled and dealt with. 
The high court rejected the RMCRA’s arguments. It said there was no evidence of the Chinese government interfering with the human rights of the residents, “even though they had strongly objected to the proposed embassy and had been involved in protests”. 
The government said it “conscientiously and carefully had regard” to the residents’ concerns. 
Ricardo Paulo Gama, a solicitor at Leigh Day, the law firm representing the residents’ association, said he hoped a higher court would be “braver” in considering the grounds of appeal. 
The RMCRA raised more than £220,000 to fund the legal challenge. The group is supported by the Inter-parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), a cross-party group of parliamentarians focused on China. skip past newsletter promotion

Luke de Pulford, the executive director of Ipac, said: “We have together already prevented the Chinese Communist party from breaking ground at Royal Mint Court for more than seven months. 
“The fight continues and we all want to win this case and to stop the embassy.” 
Mark Nygate, a representative of the RMCRA, said: “While we were also disappointed with today’s judgment, we knew this was going to be a long [process], and we intend to go all the way through.” 
Nygate said that it was a battle of “David versus two Goliaths”, the British and the Chinese governments. 
The Chinese government was not a party to the legal challenge. It has criticised the delays to the project and Xi Jinping, China’s leader, raised the matter directly with Keir Starmer, the then UK prime minister, during a phone call in 2024. 
Plans to redevelop the British embassy in Beijing have been blocked pending approval of the Chinese embassy’s new site in London .

articles.title: Could AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answer
articles.summary: Across the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods in an increasingly fragile labour market On the tree-lined streets of Wuhan, where cars jostle for space with mopeds and cargo trucks, the malfunctioning of a new type of vehicle has recently been causing chaos on the city’s roads.In March, several cars from a fleet of driverless taxis stopped abruptly in the streets. Workers and a robot prepare tea beside each other at a booth at the 2026 Zhongguancun Forum earlier this year. China’s rollout of artificial intelligence has sparked concerns about the future of the jobs market. Photograph: Jessica Lee/EPA 
View image in fullscreen 
Workers and a robot prepare tea beside each other at a booth at the 2026 Zhongguancun Forum earlier this year. China’s rollout of artificial intelligence has sparked concerns about the future of the jobs market. Photograph: Jessica Lee/EPA 
Could AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answer
Across the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods in an increasingly fragile labour market 
On the tree-lined streets of Wuhan, where cars jostle for space with mopeds and cargo trucks, the malfunctioning of a new type of vehicle has recently been causing chaos on the city’s roads. 
In March, several cars from a fleet of driverless taxis stopped abruptly in the streets. The “system malfunction” left distressed riders stranded for hours. The robotaxis, known as Apollo Go and powered by artificial intelligence (AI), were taken off Wuhan’s streets for months for investigations. 
But the outage was a boon for 45-year-old taxi driver Yao Xinnong. His wages, which had fallen by about 40% since Apollo Go launched in 2022, jumped back up as customers returned. 
“I don’t really like them, to be honest,” Yao says of the driverless cabs operated by the tech giant Baidu. “Their impact has been huge”. 
China is encouraging the deployment of AI at a scale unseen in the west. The technology is being rolled out at a staggering rate in an increasingly precarious labour market, and the Wuhan episode helped to highlight the social tensions it is causing. 
View image in fullscreen 
A Baidu driverless robotaxi on the streets of Wuhan in 2024. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images 
Gig workers like Yao are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods, while recent incidents of white-collar workers being replaced by AI have also sparked a debate over whether workers should embrace the technology – or try to compete with it. 
Addressing Shanghai’s World AI Conference in July, China’s leader, Xi Jinping, said that AI should be “an important driver for shared prosperity and common security”. 
But that goal is being pursued amid an increasingly fragile labour market. As well as suffering from high levels of unemployment, China has seen tens of millions of workers drop out of formal employment into the gig economy. According to one thinktank, the number of people in flexible employment will rise to 320 million this year, up from 160 million in 2019. That is about 44% of China’s workforce. China’s gig economy 
Taxi drivers are one part of this huge cohort. Across the country, as previously heavyweight industries such as real estate and education have floundered, workers have turned to ride-hailing apps to make ends meet. But now the rollout of robotaxis, one of the most popular applications of AI that is already in use in China, is threatening their livelihoods. 
“If the state really took you into consideration, Apollo Go would never have gone on the market,” says one Wuhan driver. 
“If things keep going this way in the future, sure, rapid development and scientific progress are great, but ordinary people like us will have no place to survive,” she adds. 
In 2024, taxi drivers in Wuhan protested against the rollout of Apollo Go in their city. It is unclear how many people took part, because news of the protests were quickly censored. Several drivers interviewed in Wuhan said they had heard about the protests but denied being involved. 
That year, a Wuhan taxi company, took the rare step of publicly criticising the government’s policy to allow automation on to the city’s streets. 
“The recent rise of autonomous ride-hailing vehicles has allowed technology to monopolise resources and take away the livelihoods of people at the bottom of society,” the letter said. 
View image in fullscreen 
Taxis wait for fares outside the airport in Wuhan, China. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images 
Authorities in China do not take kindly to public criticism. When the Guardian visited the taxi company’s office in July, an employee declined to be interviewed, citing an agreement with the police to refuse interviews and the risk of detention if he violated the agreement. 
But two years later, the government is echoing some of the same concerns first voiced by the Wuhan drivers. 
An editorial published in the state-run Workers’ Daily said that employment rights were “facing new challenges” in the age of AI. The article warned of a “collision between traditional employment rules and the iteration of AI technology”. 
The government recently pledged to “comprehensively address the impact of changes in the external environment and the development of new technologies such as artificial intelligence on employment”. 
Selina Xu, a China technology analyst, said there had been a “major vibe shift” from Beijing. 
She says that after the success of local AI model DeepSeek last year, China was “very pro AI development”. 
“This year, if you look at certain new guidelines that have been published … there has been a lot more emphasis placed on AI for boosting employment and people-first approaches,” Xu says. 
Cheng Wanhui, an official for the local government in Beijing’s hi-tech zone of Zhongguancun, says that the authorities are “paying close attention to the social issues AI brings, as well as potential ethical concerns.” 
“The key is for everyone to shift their mindset, see AI as a tool, and learn how to apply it in their future work,” Cheng says. 
Recent court rulings have awarded compensation to white-collar workers laid off by their firms to be replaced by AI. But many workers fear the AI uptake will be a barrier to them being offered a job in the first place. 
Tian Zemin, a cinematographer who works in Beijing, has worked in the film industry for nearly two decades. But now he’s out of work. “I spent six gruelling years working my way up to become a cinematographer, only to be replaced by a piece of software,” he wrote in a social media post about AI. 
“I thought I would spend my whole life in this industry. But the emergence of AI has made me feel a huge shock for the first time,” he tells the Guardian. 
Many of Tian’s peers are losing out as AI becomes more widely adopted across the film industry. His own rate as a freelancer is now 40% of what it was in 2019. 
Tian said he’s been shocked at AI’s progress. Last year, it made shonky, weird looking avatars. Now it can make convincing digital clones who have the range to carry a feature length film. “We have barely had time to react,” Tian says. 
Many analysts believe that China, where the government exerts significant control over the private sector, will be better placed than the US to contain the fallout from AI-related job losses. Beijing could for example instruct companies to comply with hiring quotas, Xu says. 
But for Tian, protections may not come soon enough. “We could be replaced at any moment,” he says. “Perhaps the only thing we can do is adapt as quickly as possible, and try to find the corner that AI still cannot replace – but that corner is getting smaller and smaller.”
